newsitem.title: INDIA: Enron says work on India unit on schedule. [CORRECTED 12:36 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Enron says work on India unit on schedule. [CORRECTED 12:36 GMT]

text.p: U.S. energy giant Enron Corp said on Saturday about 70 percent of the work on its controversial Indian power project was complete and it was hopeful of meeting the orginal schedule.

"Dabhol is about 70 percent complete and will be within months of its original completion schedule, even when we had a 14-month delay," Enron Development Corp chief executive Rebecca Mark told a business conference in the Indian capital.
Last month the company said it hoped to complete the first phase by December 1998, ahead of an earlier target date of March 1999 (corrects year from 1998).

Work on the 2,450 megawatt (MW) power plant in India's western Maharashtra state resumed late last year after the ruling Hindu nationalist government renegotiated a contract it had said was too expensive in terms of project and tariffs.
The first phase of the $2.3 billion project will generate 740 MW of electricity.
The negotiations for the Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) on the project's 1,440 MW second phase would be completed by the end of 1997, Maharashtra officials said in February.
Enron had already invested $300 million in India and more plans were underway, Mark said.
"It is not the lack of money but the procedures do not allow companies to invest more money," Mark said.
Mark said India's privatisation process has slowed down.
"This government does not have the sense of urgency and the crisis mentality needed to solve the problem," Mark said.
"Privatisation is not occurring at the pace at which it should be," she added.
Enron Corp submitted a $10 billion proposal to the Indian government last month to build power plants able to generate a total 10,000 megawatts of electricity.

The company plans to set up between five and seven power plants, ranging from 1,000 to 2,000 megawatts, in northern India as well as along the coastline in southern states, newspaper reports have said.
But Mark on Saturday refused to discuss details about the plans.

Enron's Dabhol Power Company, the firm's Indian unit, was one of eight "fast track" projects designed to lure foreign private investment into India's crumbling power sector shortly after open market reforms were launched in 1991.

Work was delayed for over a year because of a political tug-of-war between the Congress government which negotiated the contract, and the Hindu nationalist coalition which defeated it in local polls in Maharashtra state in March 1995.
It resumed late last year, after the terms of the deal were renegotiated.
